identity.title: A Generalization Result for Convergence in Learning-to-Optimize

problem.claim: Provide convergence guarantees for learned optimization algorithms in learning-to-optimize.

gap.claim: Existing convergence analysis is limited because geometric arguments for conventional optimization do not readily apply to learned algorithms, leaving theoretical guarantees mostly lacking.

contributions.claim: A probabilistic framework resembling classical optimization, designed to transfer geometric arguments to learning-to-optimize.

A generalization theorem for parametric classes of potentially non-smooth, non-convex loss functions that establishes high-probability convergence of learned optimization algorithms to critical points.
The framework places worst-case analysis in a probabilistic setting and removes the stated need for safeguards in learned-algorithm design.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a new proof strategy and a probabilistic generalization result extending convergence analysis to learned optimization algorithms and broad loss-function classes.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their main theorem establishes convergence to critical points with high probability for parametric, potentially non-smooth and non-convex loss functions.
The authors report that the result generalizes worst-case analysis into a probabilistic framework and frees learned-algorithm design from safeguards.

narrative_sequence.summary: Learning-to-optimize uses machine learning to accelerate optimization algorithms.
Despite empirical improvements over classical methods, theoretical guarantees are mostly lacking, particularly for convergence.
The authors develop a probabilistic framework resembling classical optimization so geometric arguments can be transferred to learned algorithms.
A theorem gives high-probability convergence to critical points for broad parametric loss classes, with the claimed implications for worst-case analysis and safeguards.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a specific analytical obstacle—the inapplicability of conventional geometric convergence arguments—to a framework designed to recover that style of reasoning probabilistically.

lessons.interpretation: A strong theory abstract can make the method feel motivated by explicitly mapping the identified obstacle to the mechanism intended to address it.
lessons.application: When presenting a theoretical method, state the failed or unavailable proof principle, then name the framework property that enables a corresponding proof strategy.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the work is primarily empirical or when no concrete analytical obstacle and matching mechanism are established.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the probability statement, assumptions, sample or parameter conditions, convergence notion, or definition of critical points.
It does not detail what safeguards are removed or provide quantitative comparisons with classical optimization algorithms.
